event_remark: This is a peculiar observation given prior evidence of only eggs in the diet of Drepanoides. First, perhaps the two snakes were taken as free-ranging young ones. Alternatively, perhaps they were actually ingested as eggs that were nearly ready to hatch, were liberated from their shells in the gut, and subsequently regurgitated without the shell. Finally, H. angulatus may be viviparous/ovoviviparous in southwestern Peru (Braz et al. 2016. Zoologischer Anzeiger 263: 33-44). Perhaps these two snakes were ingested just after a ovoviviparous female lay them but before they broke the membrane?

event_remark: Authors' description: "After the snake progressed forward several cm, it would raise its head 6-8 cm and rapidly and repeatedly strike (4-5 strikes observed seven times) its rostrum into the substrate. After each bout of striking, the snake would raise its head ca. 10-12 cm above the ground and observe the area it had struck. We observed this behavior for 11 min. After the seventh striking episode, the snake, while observing the substrate from the raised position, suddenly lunged forward, narrowly missing a desert iguana (Dipsosaurus dorsalis) that flushed from the area of the final striking episode. The lizard ran off with the snake in pursuit. After pursuing the lizard for ca. 5 m, the snake aborted the chase and returned to its previous foraging pattern."

event_habitat_verbatim: Inside an open enclosure used to house and reproduce green iguanas
event_remark:
The authors removed the snakes from the enclosure and placed them in a terrarium with a single iguana egg. "Subsequently, one of the snakes began piercing the shell of the egg by using its enlarged rear teeth, after which two other snakes began showing the same behavior, as each attempted to push their head
into the egg and eventually two of the snakes succeeded. The snakes then ingested the contents of the egg." Furthermore, the authors note that they have observed snakes entering the enclosure and eating iguana eggs multiple times over the past several years, with a peak occurrences in March.

event_habitat_verbatim: Permanent pond
event_remark: Observation took place on the same night the snake was observed catching and consuming calling male Dendropsophis minutus. For 20 minutes the snake remained motionless with its gazed affixed on a spot ca. 10 cm in front of it where an adult male Hypsiboas faber was sitting motionless and partially submerged. When the snake left, the frog climbed up into the aquatic vegetation and it was noted that one of its legs was injured and bleeding. The inference is that the snake unsuccessfully attempted to capture the frog, which escaped by diving into the water and remaining motionless. 2 hours later, this same snake returned to the spot and located the blood spots left by the frog as it climbed the vegetation. The snake began to inspect the blood stained vegetation where the frog still remained. The frog, observing this, fled once again to a plant half a meter away (successfully, as the snake did not notice).

event_habitat_verbatim: arboreal vegetation of a riparian forest, about 150 cm above the ground
event_remark:
"The snake (total length = 750 mm) was actively foraging when it approached a vocalizing individual of P. tetraploidea
on the arboreal vegetation of a riparian forest, about 150 cm above the ground. When the snake was about 20 cm
distant from the anuran, it sprung forward and captured the frog. For about 15 minutes, the anuran was held in
the snake’s mouth as it tried to escape. Simultaneously, the anuran used its anterior limbs to attach its adhesive
discs to the vegetation making the ingestion by the predator difficult"
reference: A record of predation and ingestion of Phyllomedusa tetraploidea (Anura, Hylidae) by Thamnodynastes strigatus (Serpentes, Dipsadidae), in the municipality of São Miguel do Oeste, state of Santa Catarina, Brazil. 2018. Herpetology Notes 11: 945-947.

event_remark: "At the time of my visit to Cuba, Dec. 13-23, 1941, it was very dry. Many of the smaller streams were a succession of puddles swarming with small fish which were being preyed upon by birds, crabs and snakes. The snakes were in turn being mutilated and even killed and eaten by the crabs. Many snakes were taken which had old or fresh scars on various parts of the body. The snakes come out of hiding about an hour after dark and start hunting fish. Snakes taken as late as 10 P.M. contained little food, but those found in the mornings resting on the mud under rocks or debris were full of fish". Unclear how many snakes he actually examined but it is clearly more than 1.

The article appears to consist of abstract only, which reads as follows:
"Lachesis muta (Viperidae) is rare, poorly known, and endemic to tropical rain forest. We observed 7 in Costa Rica; 3 were radiotagged and followed for 10-45+ days. A 90 cm female used 3 sites for 3, 6, and 25 days and moved a total of 50 m. Ca. 40% of the time over 35 days was spent alert; ca. 1% of alert time was spent moving. Days were spent under small plants, nights in an alert posture exposed on the forest floor. The 24th night she ate a rodent weighing at least 40% of her mass, remained inactive for 9 days, then moved to a new site. Observations of other L. muta (lengths 1.6-2.2 m) were consistent with these and indicate that they are very sedentary. Hunting sites were associated with Welfia palms, the seeds of which are dispersed by rodents that bushmasters eat. These snakes are extraordinarily cryptic, and move very slowly and infrequently. The hunting strategy of L. muta seems to be, find a "good" place to ambush prey, feed infrequently on large items, and minimize detection by enemies."
